   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]).    - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Serious risk: While the utility financial panel is nearly balanced (~2,072 utility-year observations across 208 utilities), employment data are completely missing for 2004, and regressions for urban domestic water supply and domestic water supply population in Table 8 drop to N = 814 (over 53% missingness relative to the N = 1,752 total urban water supply model and over 60% relative to the full panel) using complete-case analysis without missingness diagnostics (PDF pp. 7, 13, 22, 30).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious risk: Two-way fixed effects (utility and year), 1-year lagged utility and city controls, Arellano-Bond dynamic panel GMM, and a city-wide industrial profitability falsification test address time-invariant heterogeneity and observed lagged selection (such as prior profitability and road infrastructure). However, unobserved time-varying factors—including municipal leadership turnover, investor networks, and unmeasured local contractual guarantees on purchase volumes or tariff adjustments—simultaneously drive bidirectional PSP entry/exit and utility performance (PDF pp. 13-15, 17-20, 25, 31).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate: The authors accurately situate national regulatory milestones (1992 pilot opening, 2001 State Planning Committee guidelines, 2002 Ministry of Construction Circular No. 272 and 2004 Decree No. 126) and measure PSP via actual paid-in capital shares (>0% nonstate and >50% majority thresholds) rather than noisier enterprise registration labels. However, equity-share coding omits contractual PSP modes (BOT, TOT and facility divestiture), pools state-affiliated legal-entity capital with private capital, and cannot observe municipal concession terms or guaranteed-return/volume clauses (PDF pp. 7-11, 13-14, 31-32).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate risk: Operationalizing PSP strictly from utility capital structure misclassifies cities using BOT, TOT or facility divestiture concessions into the state-owned comparator group, exhibits 27 three-year back-and-forth switching anomalies attributed to potential capital coding errors, and maps city-wide yearbook water supply aggregates onto individual utilities even in multi-utility municipalities (PDF pp. 7-8, 11, 15, 23-25, 27, 32).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak to Moderate: Utility financial and productivity indicators come from standardized NBS Annual Industrial Firm Surveys, though SOE versus private accounting incentives may affect reported managerial expenses and profits. Water service outcomes rely entirely on coarse city-level yearbook aggregates (total urban water supply, urban domestic water supply and imputed domestic users derived by dividing domestic supply by per-capita use) with severe missingness and no direct measurement of water quality, pressure, nonrevenue water/leakage or retail tariffs (PDF pp. 8-9, 27, 30-32).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: No information (some concern): No pre-analysis plan or study protocol exists. Although the authors report full estimates across 12 financial indicators and 3 city water supply indicators under both raw and post-hoc corrective coding in Tables 5-8, narrative conclusions foreground preferred corrective-recoded specifications where profit-sales ratio and 10%-level domestic water user effects reach statistical significance (PDF pp. 22-31).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate risk: The sample restricts NBS Annual Industrial Firm Surveys (annual sales > 5 million CNY) to large and medium-sized utilities in prefecture-level cities—excluding small county/town utilities and defining size via employment, assets and sales—and uses manual matching across firm ID changes (often triggered by ownership restructuring) to add 60 utilities into a 208-utility panel that also retains 9 prevalent PSP utilities already privatized by 1998 (PDF pp. 6-7, 12, Section III & Table 1).

domain_ratings.justification: PSP adoption and retention are endogenous to interactions between profit-seeking investors and fiscally or infrastructurally pressured municipal governments, with Table 4 confirming positive selection on 1-year lagged profitability, liability ratio and urban road area per capita. Although two-way fixed effects, lagged covariates, Arellano-Bond GMM and a city-level industrial profit falsification test mitigate time-invariant and observed lagged confounding, the authors acknowledge that localized reform without a unified legal framework depends on unobserved idiosyncratic and time-varying factors—such as local leadership changes, investor networks and municipal commitments on guaranteed sales or tariffs—that also precipitate private-sector exits (35 exit events in Table 3) and directly affect utility revenues and performance.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: The panel is drawn from NBS Annual Industrial Firm Surveys (firms with sales > 5 million CNY in industry code 4610) restricted to medium and large utilities in prefecture-level cities defined by employment, asset and sales thresholds. Because ownership restructuring frequently caused firm ID changes, tracking by firm ID alone missed 60 restructured utilities; the authors mitigated this by manually matching firms across years on name, size, address and manager name to construct a 208-utility panel, while splitting Shanghai Water Utility Company into district utilities in 2000 and retaining 9 prevalent PSP cases already treated in 1998.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section III (PDF pp. 6-7, pp. 160-161, footnotes 5-6); Table 1 (PDF p. 12, p. 166)

domain_ratings.justification: PSP is classified contemporaneously from paid-in capital composition (any nonstate share for PSP; >50% nonstate share for PSP majority). However, three classification limitations introduce moderate bias: (1) cities engaging private operators via BOT, TOT or facility divestiture retain state capital structure and are misclassified as state-owned controls; (2) 'legal entity' capital can include investments by other state-owned or state-controlled enterprises; and (3) 27 cases switch status back and forth within 3 consecutive years due to suspected capital-source coding errors, and recoding those 27 cases materially shifts profitability estimates from null (Table 5) to statistically significant (Tables 6-7).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section III (PDF pp. 7-8, pp. 161-162, footnote 7); Section IV.A-B (PDF pp. 11, 15, pp. 165, 169, footnote 12); Section V.B (PDF pp. 23-25, pp. 177-179, Tables 5-6); Appendix Table A1 (PDF p. 32, p. 186)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: Ownership transitions are bidirectional, with 35 private-sector exits recorded between 1999 and 2007 (Table 3), often linked to unfulfilled local government commitments regarding tariff hikes or guaranteed returns/volumes. Because the panel estimator models contemporaneous PSP status (PSPit), utilities experiencing private exit immediately revert to the state-owned comparison pool without separating post-exit carryover effects, and concurrent municipal support arrangements (such as guaranteed purchase volumes or subsidies) vary across cities without direct contractual measurement.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section IV.A (PDF pp. 12-15, pp. 166-169, Table 3); Section V.A (PDF pp. 17, 20, pp. 171, 174); Section VI (PDF p. 31, p. 185)

domain_ratings.justification: Although the core financial panel has ~2,072 utility-year observations, employment is completely missing in 2004 (reducing covariate-adjusted employment and productivity models to N = 1,547 and TFP models to N = 1,507). Crucially, in the urban water service regressions (Table 8), sample size plunges from N = 1,752 for total urban water supply to N = 814 for both urban domestic water supply and domestic water supply population—over 53% missingness among otherwise included utility-years and over 60% of the full panel—analyzed via complete-case deletion with no explanation or missing-data sensitivity checks.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section III (PDF p. 7, p. 161, footnote 6); Table 2 & Figure 1 notes (PDF pp. 13-14, pp. 167-168); Table 5 (PDF p. 22, p. 176); Table 8 (PDF p. 30, p. 184)

domain_ratings.justification: Financial outcomes derive from administrative NBS firm surveys, where accounting discretion in categories such as managerial expenses and profit reporting may differ systematically after privatization. For service delivery outcomes (Section V.D), utility-level metrics are unavailable; city-wide statistical yearbook totals are assigned to sample utilities (despite multi-utility municipalities such as Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin and Chongqing), domestic user counts are imputed indirectly from aggregate domestic supply divided by per-capita domestic use, and physical leakage, water quality and pressure are unmeasured (with negative supply point estimates speculatively interpreted as leakage reductions).

domain_ratings.justification: No pre-analysis plan or prospective study protocol exists to verify pre-specification of the 12 financial indicators, 3 water service outcomes, lag structures or the post-hoc 3-year 'corrective recoding' rule. raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Jiang and Zheng (2014) conduct a 10-year longitudinal panel evaluation (1998-2007) of private sector participation (PSP) across 208 medium and large urban water utilities in 192 Chinese prefecture-level cities using NBS Annual Industrial Firm Surveys merged with China City Statistical Yearbooks. Appraised under ROBINS-I, the study has an overall Serious risk of bias, driven by two domains rated Serious (D1 Confounding and D5 Missing data) alongside Moderate risk in D2, D3, D4 and D6, and No information in D7. Specifically, although two-way fixed effects, 1-year lagged utility and city controls, Arellano-Bond dynamic panel estimators and an urban industrial profitability falsification test address time-invariant heterogeneity and observed prior profitability selection, PSP entry and frequent private-sector exits (35 exit episodes) depend on unmeasured time-varying local factors—including municipal leadership changes, investor networks and unobserved local government guarantees on purchase volumes or tariffs—creating serious residual confounding risk. Furthermore, while firm financial regressions cover ~1,500-2,072 utility-years (with 2004 employment completely missing), city-level domestic water supply and domestic user regressions drop to N = 814 (>53% missingness) with no missing-data diagnostics. Additional moderate concerns arise from misclassifying BOT/TOT/divestiture concessions as state-owned utilities, 27 three-year switching anomalies whose post-hoc recoding drives the statistical significance of profitability gains, and reliance on city-wide yearbook aggregates without direct utility-level measurements of water leakage, quality, pressure or retail tariffs.

raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study evaluates a non-randomized institutional/policy intervention—private sector participation (partial or majority nonstate equity ownership) versus continued pure state ownership in urban water utilities—using comparative longitudinal panel econometrics (two-way fixed effects and Arellano-Bond dynamic panel models). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluations with a genuine policy comparator map to ROBINS-I.
